message.content:
Civil law—often called **private or non‑criminal law**—regulates disputes between private parties (individuals, businesses, organizations) rather than offenses against society at large. Its main purpose is to resolve conflicts fairly, allocate rights and duties, and enforce obligations through judicial means when necessary. Below are its core components: | Component | What it Covers | Key Features | |-----------|-----------------|--------------| | **Sources of Law** | • Statutory laws enacted by legislatures
• Case law / precedents set by higher courts
• Administrative regulations & codes
• International treaties & conventions (when applicable)
• Customary practices recognized by courts | Determines hierarchy: statutes > binding precedent > analogous cases < customary practice. | | **Substantive Law** | Defines rights, duties, liabilities, and remedies. It’s divided into major areas:
  • Contracts – formation, performance, breach, damages
  • Torts – negligence, intentional wrongs, strict liability
  • Property – ownership, possession, transfer, easements
  • Family/Personal Status – marriage, divorce, child custody, adoption
  • Succession/Wills – inheritance rules, intestate succession
| Establishes what constitutes a valid claim and how it can be enforced. | | **Procedural Law** | Governs the process of bringing claims before courts.
- Pleadings, discovery, pre-trial motions
- Trial procedures, evidence admissibility
- Appeals, judgments, execution of orders | Ensures fairness, due process, and efficiency in dispute resolution. | | **Remedies** | Legal solutions available once a right has been infringed:
  • Civil Damages – compensatory, punitive, nominal
| Remedies aim to restore the injured party to their original position or compensate them appropriately. | | **Jurisdiction & Venue** | Rules determining which court hears a particular case based on factors like subject matter, location, parties’ residence, amount in controversy.| Prevents forum shopping and ensures proper authority over matters. | | **Enforcement Mechanisms** | How judgments are carried out:
  • Writs of attachment/seizure
  • Bankruptcy proceedings
  • Court‑ordered payments or injunction compliance monitoring
| Guarantees that decisions have practical effect beyond mere words on paper. | | **Legal Doctrine & Doctrinal Principles** | Concepts guiding interpretation and application:
  • Good faith & fair dealing
  • Doctrine of consideration (contracts)
  • Res ipsa loquitur (tort causation)
  • Statute of limitations
| Provides consistency across similar situations and helps predict outcomes. | ### How These Components Interact 1. **A plaintiff identifies a violation** under one of the substantive categories (e.g., breach of contract). 2. **They consult statutory provisions** and relevant case law to determine the exact nature of the claim and potential defenses. 3. **Pleadings are drafted**, invoking procedural requirements (notice periods, filing deadlines). 4. **Discovery and trial processes** follow procedural rules while focusing on substantive issues. 5. **Judgment renders a remedy** (damages, injunction, etc.) guided by doctrine and statutory limits. 6. **If unsatisfied, either side may appeal** following appellate procedural guidelines until the highest competent court resolves the issue. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Identify the *substance* of your claim (contract, tort, property, etc.). - [ ] Verify the governing statute(s) or contractual clauses. - [ ] Confirm you’re within the *jurisdiction* and *venue*. - [ ] Prepare pleadings per procedural standards. - [ ] Gather evidence supporting your substantive arguments. - [ ] Choose appropriate remedy(s): damages, injunctive relief, restitution, rescission. - [ ] Follow post‑judgment enforcement steps if required. Understanding each component—and how they interlock—is essential whether you're drafting a contract, litigating a personal injury suit, or navigating complex commercial disputes.

We should provide a concise overview: sources (statutes, case law), principles like contract, torts, property, family law, restitution, remedies, procedural aspects, jurisdiction, courts, enforcement mechanisms, legal doctrines, etc. Also mention civil procedure and substantive law.
